Industry News: Watch Ice Spice’s Speechless Reaction to Seeing Her Madame Tussauds Wax Figure for the First Time: ‘This Is So Accurate’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (380 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Billboard

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ice Spice got the wax-figure treatment at Madame Tussauds New York on Thursday (Nov.
  • The look sported by Ice’s figurine takes fans back to 2022 and 2023, when she was rising star working her way up the rap ranks with her signature copper curls.
  • She’s rocking a red tiger catsuit, which was donated from the “Deli” rapper’s wardrobe, along with Black Air Jordan 4s, a replica of the diamond-encrused bracelet gifted to her by Doja Cat and her Icy Princess pendant chain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ice Spice got the wax-figure treatment at Madame Tussauds New York on Thursday (Nov. 19), and the Bronx rapper was gagged at seeing her waxy twin for the first time — to the point where she was a little spooked at how the artists nailed her look, leaving her briefly speechless.

The look sported by Ice’s figurine takes fans back to 2022 and 2023, when she was rising star working her way up the rap ranks with her signature copper curls.

She’s rocking a red tiger catsuit, which was donated from the “Deli” rapper’s wardrobe, along with Black Air Jordan 4s, a replica of the diamond-encrused bracelet gifted to her by Doja Cat and her Icy Princess pendant chain.

According to recent reports, “It’s so accurate. I have a really unique face and I’m impressed they got it so right,” she remarked before later joking, “This is so accurate, like oh my God, my major-ass forehead, you literally got it.”.

Recent findings suggest that the 26-year-old posted a series of photos alongside her wax sister to social media on Friday (Nov. 20). “Put it on wax ;),” she wrote in her caption.

Ice Spice (@icespice) reacts to seeing her wax figure for the first time @TussaudsUSA pic.twitter.com/4xtw5WHdUj.

The Ice Spice wax figure will be on display at the Times Square location of Madame Tussauds Latest York in the heart of NYC into 2027.

“Ice Spice is a defining part of New York’s music and culture scene, so bringing her into Madame Tussauds New York feels especially meaningful,” mentioned Tiago Mogadouro, who serves as the general manager for Madame Tussauds New York. “She represents a new generation of artists who are shaping the city’s identity in real time, and we’re excited to give fans a way to celebrate that right here in Times Square.”.

On the music front, 2026 has been a relatively quiet year for Ice Spice. She joined forces with Lil Yachty in August for her lone release of ’26, “Out My Face (My Baby).”.

Find more footage of Ice Spice’s reaction to her wax figure below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, microsoft, the FAA, Chase, United, the NSA, and Apple all went down within one week. Officials say none of the outages were cyberattacks, but the internet isn’t buying it. This week on Uncanny Valley, WIRED senior business editor Sophie Kleeman joins Brian Barrett and Leah Feiger to discuss what actually went wrong and why people jumped straight to blaming hackers and AI. Plus, Anthropic’s historic IPO at a reported $1.5 trillion, Nvidia’s first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned, and the administration’s new rule to stop Chinese companies from renting AI chips just before Trump meets Xi.

#24633. An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an important difference between human and chimpanzee brain development.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population.
  • Although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an important difference between human and chimpanzee brain development. Researchers at Lund University have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene that remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in the developing brain.

The findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population. They also offer newly introduced clues about how the brains of humans and our closest evolutionary relatives may have developed differently.

Although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years. Some of these ancient infections left traces of viral DNA that continue to influence how genes function today.

Johan Jakobsson, Professor of Molecular Neurogenetics at Lund University, indicates the discovery demonstrates how a virus can introduce genetic changes that eventually become widespread throughout a population.

In a recent development, "The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is vital to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development," states Johan Jakobsson.

How an Ancient Virus Silenced a Brain Development Gene.

Industry observers note that at the center of the discovery is a gene called LINC00662. Researchers found that it is active during early human brain development but completely switched off in comparable chimpanzee brain models.

In a recent development, the difference appears to be caused by a genetic remnant of PTERV1, an ancient virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago. PTERV1 belongs to a group known as endogenous retroviruses, which are viruses whose genetic material became incorporated into the DNA of their hosts. Once embedded in the genome, these viral sequences can be inherited by future generations.

Recent findings suggest that over time, PTERV1 produced numerous copies of its genetic material that became scattered across different parts of the chimpanzee genome. Researchers found that these viral sequences are systematically silenced through a process called methylation.

It has been revealed that methylation involves chemical modifications to DNA that help regulate gene activity. It is one of the ways cells control which genetic instructions are used and which remain inactive. In this case, the ancient viral insertion appears to have caused a neighboring gene involved in brain development to be switched off.

Jakobsson states understanding these differences in gene regulation could also provide crucial insights into how genetic activity protects the brain or contributes to damage and disease.

Miniature Brains Reveal a Striking Genetic Difference.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate the virus's effects, researchers grew miniature brain models called organoids using stem cells from humans and chimpanzees. These three-dimensional structures reproduce certain features of developing brain tissue, allowing scientists to study aspects of early brain development under controlled laboratory conditions.

When the team compared the two types of organoids, the difference was striking. LINC00662 highlighted strong activity in the human brain models but was completely inactive in those derived from chimpanzee cells.

"The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids," says Patricia Gerdes, postdoc in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.

The researchers then set out to determine whether the ancient viral DNA was directly responsible for this difference.

Using CRISPR-Cas9, a powerful gene editing technology that allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, they removed the viral sequence from chimpanzee cells.

The result provided compelling evidence. Once the viral DNA was removed, the previously inactive LINC00662 gene switched back on.

"This shows that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees," notes Patricia Gerdes.

New Clues to Human Brain Evolution.

The team also wanted to understand what LINC00662 actually does in the human brain. To investigate, they used CRISPR to switch off the gene in human brain organoids and examined how other genes responded.

Disabling LINC00662 reduced the activity of genes associated with nerve cell development and the formation of connections between neurons. These processes are essential for establishing the networks that allow the brain to communicate and function.

The results suggest that LINC00662 contributes to notable stages of early human brain development, while the ancient viral insertion prevents the gene from functioning in chimpanzees.

According to recent reports, more broadly, the discovery highlights an notable principle of evolution. Although humans and chimpanzees share much of their genetic material, differences in how genes are switched on and off can influence how their bodies and brains develop.

The findings suggest that ancient viral infections may have contributed to these differences by altering gene regulation long after the original infections disappeared.

Researchers now plan to investigate whether other remnants of ancient viruses have similarly influenced brain evolution. They also hope to determine whether these inherited viral sequences may play a role in neurological diseases.

Together, the discoveries raise an intriguing possibility that some of the differences between human and chimpanzee brains may trace back, at least in part, to viruses that infected our evolutionary relatives millions of years ago.

Thompson—who shares kids True, 8, and Tatum, 4, with ex Khloe Kardashian—met up with Sriram Krishnan, now a Senior White House Policy Advisor on Artificial Intelligence, who he described as a "great buddy of mine.".

Industry observers note that "We're in a group chat and everyone's just talking about what they're going to do to celebrate," Thompson shared. "I stated, 'Guys, the one thing we have to do is do a dinner. We got to break bread again.'".

You should do things that you care about.".

According to Dylan Sprouse, his residuals from filming The Suite Life of Zack & Cody with twin brother Cole Sprouse is anything but suite.

"The only residual check I've ever received for The Suite Life at all was a crossover episode with Hannah Montana for five cents," the Disney Channel alum shared during a 2026 episode of his Wildmen podcast. "In a time where residuals would have been great, not a single paycheck for being arguably one of the most popular demonstrates on television.".

It has been revealed that while there's no cash prize for nabbing Dancing With the Stars' mirrorball trophy, “whoever makes it to the finale, you all get paid up until then," Jenna Johnson, who won season 33 with partner Joey Graziadei, shared. "And you do get a nice bonus.”.

According to recent reports, "If you win," Johnson, who noted pro contracts are dependent on seniority, continued. "it’s not like you get a million dollars. You’re just getting a cute trophy together.” As for those who say farewell to the ballroom early, well, as she explained, "You’re guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks.” According to multiple reports, dancer salaries start at around $1,200 to $1,600 an episode, which can increase to up to of $100,000 per season. (ABC has not confirmed these reports.) On the flip side, celebrities receive a starting salary of $125,000. As they cha-cha further into the competition, stars  receive additional bonuses with the semifinalists and finalists getting paid up to $50,000 extra.

The actress seemingly confirmed that the Friends cast—including Jennifer Aniston, Courtney Cox,David Schwimmer and Matt LeBlanc—get $20 million in residuals per year from the show re-airing, quipping to The Times in April 2026 that if she had to guess why, it's “Because Phoebe Buffay was so great?".

But in actuality, she praised the talents of her costars for their performances.

“I felt I did OK, but Jennifer and Courteney? Amazing,” she raved. “David and Matt? They had me laughing so hard. And then Matthew [Perry]—he was just beyond us all.”.

To hear Joe Giudice tell it, his and ex-wife Teresa Giudice's salary for season one of The Real Housewives of Fresh Jersey was nothing to flip over. "We got paid nothing the first season," he detailed on daughter Gia Giudice's Casual Chaos podcast in August 2025. "I'll even say, it was like $25,000. It was ridiculous. But, whatever.".

And the ingredientses they put into that initial fame-making season weren't cheap. "I think the first year we had that big party in my great room," the father of four reflected. "I think that show cost me $150,000 the first year.".

Oprah Winfrey happily accepted only a little bit of green to star in 1985’s The Color Purple.

Industry observers note that “They were only offering $35,000 to be in this film, and it is the best $35,000 I ever earned,” the billionaire media mogul told Essence in 2023. “It changed everything and taught me so much.”.

The actress revealed that she made about $20,000 per episode of Two and a Half Men with a 5 percent raise each season, making about $43,000 for one episode in the final season.

When she scored the role of late Tejana singer Selena Quintanilla in the 1997 biopic Selena, Jennifer Lopez became the first Latina actress to earn $1 million for a film.

According to recent reports, “I was too young and didn’t know what the hell was going on,” Lopez told Variety in 2019, reflecting on her breakout movie. “It was great they offered me a million dollars. I feel like everyone was making a statement.”.

And it paved the way for her to make hundreds of millions more, though sometimes her participation doesn’t cost a thing.

“I do things because I love them,” Lopez explained to GQ in 2019. “I didn't get paid a whole bunch of money for Hustlers. I did it for free and produced it. I bank on myself, you know? Like Jenny From the Block—I do what I love.".

Recent findings suggest that adrien Brody didn’t do The Brutalist for the money. Rather, he took on the role of a Hungarian architect suffering for his art in post-WWII America for $250,000 and won his second Oscar for Best Actor.

“I need a studio movie now, because I’ve poured it all into this,” Brody quipped to Variety, referring to the “barn that looks like a castle” he’s renovating in upstate Newly introduced York.

“Do you guys know what they pay us?” Pete Davidson cracked to Upcoming York magazine when asked ahead of Saturday Night Live's 50th anniversary special how he spent his money when he was first hired at the age of 20 in 2014. “It’s like three grand an episode, so I think I got dinner.”.

It has been revealed that interestingly, the salaries have remained proportional for SNL newcomers, with season one stars John Belushi, Jane Curtin, Gilda Radner, Dan Aykroyd and Chevy Chase reportedly earning $750 an episode back in 1975. Which was roughly equivalent to $3,300 in 2014, according to the Consumer Price Index Inflation calculator. (Though the $750 of 1975 is $4,428 in 2025.).

While Kenan Thompson makes a lot more than $3,000 per episode of SNL now that he’s in his record 22nd season, the former Nickelodeon star had to start somewhere.

Recent findings suggest that “That first commercial when they paid me, it was $800,” the All That alum revealed in Demi Lovato‘s 2024 documentary Child Star. “I was 12 so that may as well have been a million dollars.".

It turns out Gilmore Girls’ status as a beloved rewatchable classic is literally priceless.

“There really are no residuals on Netflix,” Lauren Graham, who played Lorelai Gilmore for seven seasons and then reprised the role for 2016’s Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life, remarked on Jimmy Kimmel Live in March 2025. “But I’ve been paid in love and appreciation.”.

Feeling not so appreciated, Tommy Dorfman got specific about her 13 Reasons Why paycheck during the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike—which was prompted in part (as was the WGA strike) by streamers like Netflix not making it a practice to pay additional compensation to cast and crew once a show had become a significant hit.

"my earnings for the entire first season of 13 reasons why were $29,953.24 prior to agency and manager fees (20%) and taxes," Dorfman wrote on Threads July 24. "8 episodes over six months." She continued, “i did all of the promo and had KEY ART for this show, flew round trip from NYC to SF to shoot for every episode, was kept for days without pay/working. i barely qualified for insurance.".

And, Dorfman added, “within the first 28 days of release, the show's season 1 garnered a total of 476 million view hours. this is why we strike.".

Without naming names or numbers, Dax Shepard told fellow Parenthood alum Lauren Graham when she appeared on his podcast that he knew he made “among the lowest of all the actors” on their NBC drama, which ran for six seasons.

But, the Armchair Expert host stressed that he did not mind.

“Every job I had ever had in my life prior to Parenthood, I made a point to find out what everyone was making,” he said. “I'd always figure it out—either a conversation where I get it out of them or I backchannel through an agent.".

So he made a point to purposely not seek out such info about his Parenthood family, which helped with enjoying the experience even when he did get an inkling of where he was on the pay pyramid.

“I got a dollar for writing the script,” George Clooney told the Los Angeles Times in 2005 about the financial strings he pulled to get his film Good Night, and Good Luck made. “I had to endorse my check for directing and turn in my acting salary. [Actor, cowriter and coproducer Grant Heslov] and I each made a buck for doing it.”.

Sources indicate that his labor of love about CBS News journalist Edward R. Murrow speaking truth to power in the 1950s had legs, though: Making his Broadway debut, Clooney wrapped his months-long stint playing Murrow in a stage adaptation of the film  in June 2025. And with the play having grossed a Broadway record (for a nonmusical) $3.3 million during a preview week before it officially opened April 3, he made a lot more than $1.

For his chilling turn as Patrick Bateman in 2000’s American Psycho, Christian Bale was paid “the absolute minimum they were legally allowed to pay me” because no one in the production really wanted to hire him except director Mary Harron, the Welsh actor told GQ in 2022.

He made so little, Bale shared, that he remembered “sitting in the makeup trailer and the makeup artists were laughing at me because I was getting paid less than any of them.”.

No, the Game of Thrones cast didn't get paid $300,000 per episode, according to Emilia Clarke.

“We didn’t earn that much," she told Variety in 2026. "Can you imagine? I’d have been driving a couple of Porsches!".

However, the actress—who played Daenerys Targaryen for eight seasons between 2011 and 2019—noted that the money she made throughout the HBO show did provide her with enough financial security to pay off her parents’ mortgage.

His uncle may have been Rico, but Jon Heder confirmed in 2010 that he was “initially” only paid $1,000 for Napoleon Dynamite.

After the irreverent comedy became a sleeper hit, he was able to renegotiate for a piece of the profits, telling the New Zealand Herald, “They went a little bit higher.”.

Djimon Hounsou mentioned he’s “definitely underpaid” in Hollywood despite his prestigious list of credits, including Amistad and Blood Diamond.

According to recent reports, "I've been in this business and making films now over two decades," the Beninese actor told CNN’s Larry Madowo in January 2025. "And still—with two Oscar nominations and been in many significant blockbuster films—and yet I’m still struggling financially to make a living.".

Rebel Wilson detailed in her 2024 memoir Rebel Rising that she was paid $3,500 to do Bridesmaids, “a fee that I then had to pay directly to the Screen Actors Guild to join the union. So really, I got paid nothing.”.

Still, she wrote, the experience was “everything!”.

In a recent development, and the Australian actress’ star rose ever a-ca higher, with her fee going from the SAG minimum scale of $65,000 for 2012’s Pitch Perfect to $10 million for 2017’s Pitch Perfect 3. Wilson wrote that she raked in $20 million total for the threequel, Isn’t It Romantic and The Hustle, though—reality alert—she “lost almost 50 percent to taxes, 10 percent to agents and 5 percent” to her lawyer. But even after those obligations and paying her publicist, business manager and assistant, Wilson “netted what to me was an absolute fortune.”.

In late 2017, Ellen Pompeo negotiated a latest Grey’s Anatomy contract for $575,000 per episode, a seven-figure signing bonus and two full backend equity points worth an estimated $6 million to $7 million.

It has been revealed that “I’m 48 now, so I’ve finally gotten to the place where I’m OK asking for what I deserve, which is something that comes only with age,” Pompeo told The Hollywood Reporter in 2018. “Because I’m not the most ‘relevant’ actress out there. I know that’s the industry perception because I’ve been this character for 14 years. But the truth is, anybody can be good on a show season one and two. Can you be good 14 years later? Now, that’s a f--kin’ skill.”.

Reflecting more recently on how she always made less than costar Patrick Dempsey, even though she was the Grey in question, Pompeo said she didn’t begrudge him his money.

According to recent reports, but, she noted on a March 2025 episode of Call Her Daddy, “Just being that I was the namesake of the show, I deserved the same and that was harder to get. I wasn't salty about him getting what he got. I was salty that they didn't value me as much as they valued him and they never will.”.

Sources indicate that jamie Lee Curtis recalled getting paid $2,000 a week—so $8,000 in total—for 1978’s Halloween, her movie debut. “I mean,” she told Rotten Tomatoes in 2018, “nobody got paid, anything.”.

Sources indicate that yet while the scream queen earned four figures, director John Carpenter’s friend Nick Castle felt like a king making $25 per day to share the role of Michael Myers. (It’s Anthony Moran whose face you see when the killer’s mask comes off for a freaky second, and editor Tommy Lee Wallace also logged screentime as Michael.).

“That was a lot at the time!” Castle, who attended film school at USC with Carpenter, told Vanity Fair in 2018. “You have to remember: My interest in doing the film was being on set, so I could demystify the experience of filmmaking and directing. I expected to hang around the set for no money. But hey, $25 per day, and all I had to do was wear a rubber mask.”.

Taraji P. Henson earned a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nomination for 2008’s The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, but years later she was still fired up by the $150,000 she accepted to be in the movie—after producers rejected the $500,000 quote she brought to the table.

As for the film’s leads Brad Pitt and Cate Blanchett, “You don’t hear a lot of $20 million quotes anymore, but at this time that was happening,” Henson remarked on the Ladies First With Laura Brown podcast in 2021. “And rightfully so—I’m not saying they shouldn’t have paid Cate and Brad what they deserved.”.

Recent findings suggest that but, she continued, “I’m bringing a certain amount to the seat too and I felt like what I was asking at that time in my career was fair, was fair to the ticket sales that I would contribute to this massive film. Wouldn’t do it.” Henson was “gutted” when they offered $100,000, she recalled. “When it was all remarked and done I got $150,000, but I had to swallow my pride, baby.”.

Recent findings suggest that breaking it down, “I know people go, ‘$150,000, that’s a lot of money!’” Henson acknowledged. “I don’t ever want people to think that I’m ungrateful because that is not me.” But, she calculated, “Uncle Sam is going to take 50 percent of that, so now you’re left with, what? $75,000. Now before Uncle Sam takes the money, I have to pay my team before taxes, 30 percent. So once Uncle Sam takes his 75, then I got another 30 that’s coming off of that 75, so I may have made $40,000?”.

While Blanchett has made plenty of money over the years, it didn’t all come from playing royal elf Galadriel in The Lord of the Rings franchise, though it grossed $2.9 billion at the worldwide box office.

“Are you kidding me? No,” she retorted on Watch What Happens Live in August 2024 when Andy Cohen guessed LOTR was her biggest paycheck. “No one got paid anything to do that movie…I mean, I basically got free sandwiches, and I got to keep my ears.”.

They weren’t paid a precious amount, that is. Orlando Bloom, who played elven warrior Legolas, shared on The Howard Stern Show in 2023 that he made $175,000 for the whole trilogy.

Hopefully he also got to keep his ears.

Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that last year, GOP Rep.
  • Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

It has been revealed that last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has revealed looks to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”.

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go.

It has been revealed that in the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.).

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.).

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.).

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”.

Trump's risky call for protests.

In a recent development, greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”.

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.).

Join us on Twitter and Facebook.

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”.

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

Novo states Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.
  • Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.

Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial.

When evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.

The detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications.

"This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," said Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity.

According to recent reports, in 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040.

While Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are at the moment no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6.

It has been revealed that in Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.

Industry observers note that but more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September.

"We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina mentioned.

Novo said Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The firm added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids.

Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said.

"That is something that is still an evidence gap," she remarked, pointing to the potential of future research.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alex Consani is ready for a spin around Vice City.

With the supermodel lending her voice to Grand Theft Auto VI—which is poised to be the biggest video game of the year after making $3.79 billion in preorder and first-day sales, according to parent firm Take Two—it was only appropriate that she channel that car vibe into her clutch look for the game’s launch party.

Consani buckled up for the Nov. 18 event at the Gekko restaurant in Miami wearing a short dress from Paris-based label Sevali’s spring 2025 collection that was made out of upcycled seatbelts. The belts crisscrossed around the 23-year-old’s svelte figure, coming to a click—literally—with a buckle that was strapped across her shoulder.

The Victoria’s Secret model completed her look with clear kitten heels and her long blonde hair parted down the middle and flowing behind her.

In the newly released video game, Consani can be heard as a DJ for the in-game radio station Flash FM alongside singer Robyn. The two play songs from the likes of Olivia Rodrigo, Charli XCX, Zara Larsson and more as they put their commentary into high gear.

After playing Rodrigo’s “good 4 u,” Consani can be heard saying in a clip posted from the game, “How do you even fumble a baddie like Olivia?”.

According to recent reports, she also had some love for Charli XCX, saying, “Whatever Charli XCX does, she’s my medicine. That is my f--king doctor, y’all.”.

Sources indicate that as for Larsson? After playing the Swedish singer’s hit “Fast Emotion,” Consani commented, “God, I love Zara so much.”.

#24627. Latest Update: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (958 w)

Latest Update: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible.
  • Sources indicate that the findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a upcoming puzzle.
  • According to recent reports, atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible. Using radio waves, they managed to directly control the magnetic spin of the nucleus inside a single atom. The unexpected result challenges existing assumptions about how atomic magnetism behaves and could eventually lead to new ways of storing and retrieving quantum information.

Sources indicate that the findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a upcoming puzzle. Although the experiment demonstrated that this remarkable level of control is possible, researchers do not yet fully understand the mechanism that makes it work.

The Hidden Magnetism Inside Every Atom.

According to recent reports, atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets. However, the magnetism within an atom comes from different sources. Both electrons and, in some cases, the atomic nucleus possess a quantum property called spin, which can be thought of as a miniature magnetic compass needle.

"By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons," states lead researcher Sander Otte. "But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world.".

That protection makes nuclear spin especially interesting to quantum researchers. Because it is less exposed to disturbances from its surroundings, it could offer a promising way to preserve delicate quantum information.

To investigate these tiny magnetic properties, Otte's team uses a specially modified scanning tunneling microscope. This powerful instrument allows the researchers to deliver electrical signals to individual atoms with extraordinary precision.

Recent findings suggest that until recently, their experiments concentrated primarily on electron spin because it is easier to detect and measure. The nucleus's magnetic spin could only be observed indirectly through a phenomenon known as the hyperfine interaction, which creates a subtle quantum connection between the spins of the electron and nucleus. This connection can cause the two spins to become slightly entangled, meaning their quantum states are linked.

An Atomic Experiment Produces an Unexpected Result.

In the latest study, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues took a different approach. They simultaneously applied two separate signals to a single atom, with one directed at the electron and the other at the nucleus.

Sources indicate that by using these signals together, the researchers could investigate their effects independently. What happened next caught them by surprise.

According to recent reports, even when the electron and nuclear spins were largely disentangled, the team was still able to flip the orientation of the nucleus's magnetic spin. Based on their previous understanding, the nucleus should not have responded in this way.

"According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen," says Otte. "The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope.".

The result suggests that the interaction between electrical signals and nuclear spin involves a mechanism that scientists have yet to fully explain.

Controlling Quantum Spins Like Guitar Strings.

It has been revealed that achieving this level of precision required the researchers to adapt a technique called double magnetic resonance so it could operate on a single atom. The method allowed them to manipulate the magnetic behavior of the atomic nucleus separately from that of an electron.

Magnetic resonance works by applying a wave signal at a carefully selected frequency to change the orientation of a magnetic spin. However, quantum mechanics restricts these changes to specific allowed transitions, meaning the frequency must be precisely matched to the spin being targeted.

Vennema compares the process to playing a musical instrument.

According to recent reports, "You can compare it to the strings of a guitar," Vennema explains. "Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The "notes" of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin.".

Recent findings suggest that in other words, electrons and atomic nuclei respond to very different frequencies, much as different guitar strings produce different musical notes. By tuning their signals to the appropriate frequencies, the scientists could address the two types of spin separately.

A Quantum Breakthrough With a Mystery Still to Solve.

The discovery could have crucial implications for the future of quantum information technology. Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum systems can use quantum states to encode information in more complex ways.

One major challenge is keeping those states stable long enough for information to be stored and retrieved reliably. Nuclear spins are attractive candidates for quantum memory because they are relatively well isolated from environmental interference.

The ability to control these spins directly could therefore open upcoming possibilities for writing, storing, and reading quantum information. However, the findings represent an early experimental advance rather than a ready-to-use quantum memory technology.

For now, one of the most important outcomes is the new scientific mystery the experiment has revealed. The researchers have demonstrated an unexpected way to manipulate nuclear spin, but the physical mechanism responsible remains unclear.

"Back to the drawing board, then," claims Otte. "That is really how science works. There is always something latest left to figure out.".

  • But can making small gestures of affection in a video game actually teach players anything about being a better partner IRL?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that since Rockstar released previews of Grand Theft Auto VI this summer, social media has buzzed about the relationship system at the heart of the game. While some critics jumped to say that playing GTA 6 is cheating on your significant other, others speculated that playing the game might actually make players better at IRL connections — especially considering that young adults have less experience.

Now that GTA 6 is out, discussion of the latter has resurfaced on X:.

But can making small gestures of affection in a video game actually teach players anything about being a better partner IRL? To answer that question, I reached out to sex and couples therapist Ilana Grines, whom I previously spoke to about whether playing the game is cheating.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections.

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups.

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups.

Pure — best for anonymous hookups.

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

According to recent reports, "We have to be really careful about what we're claiming that video games can actually do for us," Grines said. It's useful when individuals are exposed to behaviors that are typically associated with relationship satisfaction as a whole — like spending time together — but, she said, "your girlfriend doesn't have a meter on her forehead that increased the more you...show her attention.".

Industry observers note that part of the online conversation stems from the relationship between GTA 6 protagonists Jason and Lucia, whose connection develops through the player's actions. While players can choose to keep their relationship platonic, the game still tracks their bond. Holding hands, buying flowers, giving compliments, sending texts, and running errands together (which may or may not involve committing crimes) can all improve their relationship score.

In a recent development, the relationship meter gives players a sense of where Jason and Lucia stand with one another, Mashable's editorial director Eric Miller explained to me, a self-professed non-gamer. While previous GTA games have featured romantic relationships and family dynamics, GTA 6 takes things a step further by allowing players to actively shape the protagonists' relationship. Depending on their actions, Jason and Lucia can be running on empty (1/4), partners in crime (2/4), crazy in love (3/4), or hot together (4/4).

Grines is skeptical that simply performing these actions in a game can teach emotional intelligence. "You're literally playing a game when you could be participating in your relationship," Grines continued. That's another line of thinking that's echoed on social media today: That people (mostly men) are doing chores for Lucia instead of their IRL girlfriend.

Sources indicate that one of Grines' clients told her that his girlfriend isn't letting him buy the game — but not because of Lucia. It's actually because of the strip club scenes and how realistic the characters look. The girlfriend isn't comfortable with him going to strip clubs in real life, so why would she be comfortable with him going to one in a video game? As in our discussion over whether playing GTA 6 is cheating, Grines said she's entitled to set a boundary.

According to recent reports, real relationships, of course, are more complicated than any in-game relationship meter can capture. And Grines warns against having unrealistic expectations for how video games can improve romance. While seeing a healthy relationship modeled in front of you can be useful, she said that modeling doesn't always create behavioral change. Being a good boyfriend in the game doesn't factor in a real partner's own preferences, emotions, and agency. (For example, your real girlfriend may hate flowers!).

According to recent reports, that doesn't mean GTA 6 can't bring couples closer together. Gaming can be a shared experience, as PCMag's Jordan Minor demonstrated when he played the game with his wife.

"It's great that people can experiment and they can repeat actions that may improve their relationship satisfaction," she noted. "The real test will be if they can take it out of the video game and into their real lives.".

Sources indicate that not everyone likes this element of the game. Right-wing (or right-wing adjacent) influencers Asmongold and Clavicular (who was indicted on two rape charges yesterday) expressed their distaste for GTA 6. The former called the game a "cuck simulator" while playing it on stream, and Clavicular said the game is "insanely cucked.".

Then again, GTA 6 is the highest-rated game of all time, so the haters are in the minority.

According to recent reports, anna Iovine is the associate editor of features at Mashable. Previously, as the sex and relationships reporter, she covered topics ranging from dating apps to pelvic pain. Before Mashable, Anna was a social editor at VICE and freelanced for publications such as Slate and the Columbia Journalism Review. Follow her on Instagram.

In the wake of that release, which blended traditional Argentine folkloric influences into his sound, he began playing arenas and stadiums in Spanish-speaking markets. Earlier this year, he took home 13 trophies at Premios Gardel — Argentina’s equivalent of the Grammys — including artist of the year. He won four Latin Grammys at this year’s ceremony, including record of the year, and has been nominated for two 2027 Grammys, including best Latin song (“Niño”) and best Latin rock/alternative album (La Vida Era Más Corta).

Recent findings suggest that among other recent milestones, Milo recently performed on The Tonight Show With Jimmy Fallon. He’s slated to perform at a crop of upcoming events including Vive Latino, Coachella, Isle of Light, Panama Crossroads and Estéreo Picnic. He’ll also soon headline his first shows in Brazil, including at the Rock in Rio festival, as well as shows across Central America at 7,000-17,000-capacity venues and at a stadium in Córdoba, Argentina.

Milo is managed by his mother, attorney Aldana Ríos.

#24622. Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal.
  • But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
  • As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.

But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.

As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.

They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).

Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.

The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.

Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find fresh forms of income.

A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.

Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.

It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.

"I think it's more of a long-term game," mentioned Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.

She claims it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it reveals it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.

One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels.".

She says it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF plans and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.

The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott remarked.

This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.

It has been revealed that since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national looks to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no latest commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.

Recent findings suggest that kumar says more countries could announce similar plans just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.

Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.

Industry observers note that the nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.

The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.

The roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.

Industry observers note that kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.

This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any massive announcements about fossil fuels.

According to recent reports, global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.

A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald shows that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing new reserves.

Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.

It has been revealed that one issue Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.

The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.

Ideally, Kumar stated, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.

"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum.".

Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity.
  • Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image reveals the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away.
  • It has been revealed that the image of this black hole, designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity, which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like.

Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image reveals the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away.

It has been revealed that the image of this black hole, designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all?

Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky.

"It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai remarked in a statement sent to Space.com via email.

In a recent development, lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an notable step in the scientific process.".

This could settle the questions of just how the final image of M87* was influenced by both atmospheric effects and the processing methods needed to reconstruct pictures from telescope data.

That's not just good news for the EHT; it's good news for Einstein.

Industry observers note that einstein published his theory of general relativity in 1915, completely reshaping how we think of gravity. General relativity suggested that objects with mass curve the very fabric of space and time, united as a single entity called spacetime. Gravity arises from that curvature.

According to recent reports, the greater the mass, the more extreme the curvature and thus the greater the gravitational influence of that object. Taking this to its extreme, scientist Karl Schwarzschild came up with a solution to the equations of general relativity that suggested an infinitesimal region with infinite mass, resulting in unrestrained curvature, a singularity. Around this would be a spherical boundary at which not even light has the velocity needed to escape this region. Referred to as the Schwarzschild radius, that boundary became known as the event horizon of a black hole. The singularity, its heart. Black holes were born in 1915, decades before their discovery and over a century before the EHT saw one.

General relativity also predicted what the region around the event horizon would look like. A ring of superheated glowing plasma with the shadow of the black hole falling on it.When scientists first saw the image of M87* they were astounded at how close it reflected predictions made by general relativity, thus confirming the the theory once again. This verification further solidifies that development.

Verifying the EHT's image of M87* could lead to the CSIRO-developed technique being applied to some more "down-to-Earth" uses such as improving medical imaging and mapping earthquakes.

"Independent validation is at the heart of the scientific process, and it is especially valuable for results as novel as those of the EHT. It is extremely gratifying to see that GenDIReCT, an elegant, entirely independent method, recovers the ring structure of M87* across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration’s published results," Laurent Loinard, Director of the EHT Collaboration, stated.

"Studies like this strengthen our confidence in what we have learned about black holes, and enrich the toolkit available to the whole community.".

The team's research was published on Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature.

Recent findings suggest that robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, Latest Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #24619. A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1409 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising latest way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to fresh treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
  • The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising latest way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to fresh treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

In Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's.

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

Previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," said Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease.".

To investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage.

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

According to recent reports, one notable effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

Industry observers note that the protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

Beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," stated Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see.".

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse.

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

Sources indicate that SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

In a recent development, the results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

"The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," said Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies.".

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an important protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A Latest Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments.

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

Sources indicate that they combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis highlighted that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

Industry observers note that the researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," mentioned Huijie Huang.

Plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

"There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," noted Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies.".

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research.

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

Sources indicate that the team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

"Mouse cells and human cells are different," mentioned Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment.".

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

According to recent reports, ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal newly introduced treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, veteran record label executive Mort Weiner died on Oct. 25 at age 92. Over a career spanning nearly four decades, Weiner held senior positions in sales, promotion, marketing and distribution at several major record labels, including Columbia, MGM, Metromedia, Motown, RCA and 20th Century-Fox Records.

Veteran music executive Neil Portnow, former president/CEO of the Recording Academy, tells Billboard, “Mort was a colleague from my first days in L.A. at RCA in the late ‘70’s, and then at 20th Century Fox Records where I hired him to run our marketing, sales and international efforts. I couldn’t have made a better choice because his work, energy and commitment to artists and our industry were superb. But most importantly, I gained a true friendship which has lasted through these many decades. He will be missed by all who had the privilege to work with and know him.”.

Weiner began his record company career in 1961 as the Miami branch manager for Dot Records, which had a No. 1 hit on the Billboard Hot 100 that year with Pat Boone’s “Moody River.” He went on to handle local promotion for Columbia Records in Miami, where he helped build early interest in Simon & Garfunkel. In 1966, he took responsibility for promotion across 11 Southern states for Columbia’s Date label. He joined MGM and was named national singles sales manager for Verve and Verve/Forecast in 1967.Weiner joined Metromedia Records around the time of its launch in late 1968 and rose from Eastern regional promotion to director of national sales and then to national director of marketing and merchandising. The label’s biggest star was Bobby Sherman, one of the top teen pop stars of the era. Sherman landed four top 10 Hot 100 hits for Metromedia from 1969-70, including “Easy Come, Easy Go” and “Julie, Do Ya Love Me.”Weiner joined Motown Records in its Los Angeles office, where he served as executive administrator of promotion. His tenure included the label’s Anthology franchise, which drew on Motown’s priceless catalog. The Anthology series began in 1973 with a Temptations collection that rode the Billboard 200 for six months and went platinum. While at Motown, Weiner was named a finalist for record company executive of the year at Bobby Poe’s Radio/Record Seminar and Awards Banquet.In 1975, Weiner moved to RCA as the sales and promotion manager for custom labels. He went on to direct custom label sales and, in 1977, became director of pop product merchandising, overseeing RCA’s pop product managers. His work with affiliated labels included Silver Convention’s “Fly, Robin, Fly” on Midland International (a Hot 100-topping, Grammy-winning smash from 1975), the soundtrack to The Omen on Tattoo Records, and releases by The Whispers and Carrie Lucas on Soul Train Records. Jefferson Starship thanked him in the credits to its 1978 album Earth, which made the top five on the Billboard 200 and went platinum.In 1979, Weiner joined 20th Century-Fox Records as director of sales and merchandising. He became vp of sales and merchandising in 1980. That same year, label president Portnow put him in charge of international operations. As part of the label’s push to expand sales abroad, Weiner met with executives at RCA, which handled the label’s international distribution. In an October 1980 Billboard interview, Portnow pointed to singer-songwriter Jim Photoglo’s success in Japan as an example of the label’s increased presence overseas.Weiner later served as vp of sales and distribution at Total Experience Records, where he helped introduce a program that used lower suggested retail prices and dealer incentives to support new artists. He returned to Motown in 1987 as vp of sales and distribution, a newly created position at the time. Smokey Robinson had back-to-back top 10 hits on the Hot 100 that year: “Just to See Her” (which won a Grammy) and “One Heartbeat.” Weiner’s later work took him into record and compact disc manufacturing, including a role as vp of sales at Nimbus Manufacturing.From his early days promoting singles in Miami to his work in national distribution and CD manufacturing, Weiner spent his career on the business side of getting music heard.

Weiner is survived by his wife Sharron; his children Timothy, Melinda, and Mark; and nine grandchildren.
