Industry News: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function.
  • The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less key than how they use that time.
  • The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less key than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially notable because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills.

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Sources indicate that cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn upcoming things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

According to recent reports, the findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently.

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Industry observers note that working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing newly introduced information.

Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity.

Sources indicate that the study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

It has been revealed that one possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

Sources indicate that "Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

Industry observers note that "However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is key to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

What the Eight-Year Study Revealed.

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

It has been revealed that importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

Latest Update: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

📅 05 Oct 2022 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios declared on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.
  • This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.
  • The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios declared on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival.".

Recent findings suggest that based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​.

In a recent development, the first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond.".

Industry observers note that shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

According to recent reports, in principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their intends.

Sources indicate that although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Recent findings suggest that whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Recent findings suggest that aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

In a recent development, another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Industry observers note that smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral.".

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary.".

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian.".

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17.".

Recent findings suggest that pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions.
  • We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance.
  • Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A total solar eclipse will sweep across the country, passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date.

We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps.

Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it. When an ancient text reliably describes an eclipse, it can anchor a moment in history to a specific place and time.

It has been revealed that we know from astronomical calculations that eclipses crossed Egypt long before anyone left an identifiable written record of one. On April 1, 2471 B.C., a total solar eclipse swept across northern Egypt during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that the eclipse may help explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf broke with tradition and built a huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. It's a tantalizing hypothesis, but no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse.

Astronomers can calculate that an eclipse happened, but using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that someone actually saw it and recorded it. That's where an eclipse almost 1,300 years later becomes particularly intriguing.

According to recent reports, A passage in the Old Testament book of Joshua describes the sun and moon as if they stopped in the sky. After leading the people of Israel into Canaan — modern-day Israel and Palestine — Joshua prayed: "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies." Ancient Gibeon is about six miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.

According to recent reports, in research published in 2017, researchers Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington at Cambridge University in the U.K. claimed it could refer to an annular solar eclipse on Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. It's a controversial interpretation, not least because it depends on exactly how the ancient Hebrew text is translated. However, if correct, it could be the oldest recorded solar eclipse with a date that has been identified — and it could also more accurately date the reign of Ramesses II. Also known as Ramesses the Great, he reigned for 66 years during Egypt's Latest Kingdom, commissioned Abu Simbel, made major additions to Karnak and Luxor Temple, and lived to be over 90. His reign marked the final peak of ancient Egyptian imperial power. According to the BBC, he is the "Jupiter" of the pharaonic system. However, the precise dates of his reign remain subject to debate, with historians using a combination of archaeological, historical and astronomical evidence to reconstruct the chronology.

Sources indicate that now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, the Merneptah Stele is a large inscribed granite monument written in the fifth year of Pharaoh Merneptah's reign, successor to Ramesses II. Discovered in 1896 at Merneptah's mortuary temple on the west bank of the Nile, opposite modern-day Luxor, it describes an Egyptian military campaign in Canaan and mentions Israelites. Egyptologists generally date Merneptah's reign to around 1213 — 1203 B.C., placing his fifth year around 1209/1208 B.C. That means the Israelites were already living in Canaan by then.

Sources indicate that using calculations that accounted for changes in Earth's rotation over thousands of years, Humphreys and Waddington identified an annular eclipse visible from Canaan for five minutes on the afternoon of Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. If the biblical passage does describe this event, that's a fixed astronomical date that could be used to refine the chronology of the Egyptian pharaohs. The researchers proposed that it occurred during the second, third or fourth year of Merneptah's reign.

If Humphreys and Waddington's interpretation of the biblical text is correct, the eclipse of 1207 B.C. could be the oldest solar eclipse identified in a written record. The researchers propose that Ramesses II reigned from approximately 1276 to 1210, with an uncertainty of about a year, slightly different from the conventional dates of 1279-1213 B.C. used by the British Museum.

Industry observers note that so an eclipse can be like a timestamp on an undated photograph, but this one does not show that the book of Joshua actually describes an eclipse. The interpretation of the Hebrew has been challenged by Marinus Anthony van der Sluijs, whose paper argues that the biblical narrative states that the sun was standing over Gibeon and the moon was over the Valley of Aijalon simultaneously — so not an eclipse at all.

Sources indicate that on Aug. 2, 2027, there will be no such ambiguity. We already know where the moon's shadow will cross Egypt, when it will reach Luxor and how long darkness will last. Almost 4,500 years separate that eclipse from the one that crossed Egypt in 2471 B.C. and 3,233 years from 1207 B.C., but both are movements of the same celestial clock. Run it forwards, and it predicts the future. Run it backward, and occasionally an eclipse of the sun can put a date on history.

There were significantly fewer flight delays and cancellations Monday than had been reported Sunday, according to FlightAware data.

There was no indication that United's outage Monday was related to the problems that caused Friday's ground stop.

#24567. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal notable differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
  • The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism showed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal notable differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies.

To explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

It has been revealed that movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Recent findings suggest that using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies.".

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages.

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

According to recent reports, at first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

In a recent development, people with autism revealed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

In a recent development, this increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research.

According to recent reports, the results raise key questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?".

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support.".

Industry observers note that the researchers now blueprint to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

Awards Circuit Podcast: The roundtable discusses “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” and the casting of Robert Pattinson as James Bond.

The reason so many of us cried at “Project Hail Mary” has five legs, no face and a voice that belongs to James Ortiz. And he’s so damn effective.

Sources indicate that in April, Variety exclusively reported that Amazon MGM would submit Ortiz for best supporting actor at the 99th Academy Awards for his performance as Rocky. We’ve written plenty of consideration stories. None has produced what that one did: TikToks, Instagram Reels and a corner of film Twitter demanding, with real passion, that someone “get this adorable rock creature nominated for an Oscar immediately,” as Mike Sawicki of the “Mike, Mike and Oscar” YouTube channel and podcast put it. The groundswell even made it to NBC’s “Today,” where Carson Daly spotlighted it.

Months later, sitting in the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast studio, Ortiz still sounds like he’s processing all of it. “Did this actually happen?” he states with a wince. “It feels like it happened to somebody else two years ago.”.

In a recent development, on this episode, Ortiz talks about bringing Rocky to life through his puppet artistry, from the eight weeks his team spent turning subtext into movement to the hours of reference footage that guided Framestore’s animators. He also lays out what he wants from Hollywood when it comes to recognizing and protecting puppetry work, why Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s set felt like “putting on a play in their parents’ garage” and the “Batman Forever” obsession that shaped him as a kid.

Lord and Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s novel opened in March to $80.5 million domestically, a record for Amazon MGM and went on to gross more than $680 million worldwide, the non-franchise phenomenon the theatrical business had been praying for. At its center, opposite Ryan Gosling’s Ryland Grace, sits Rocky, the Eridian engineer built by Neal Scanlan’s creature shop and performed on set by Ortiz and a team of puppeteers he assembled. He was hired to operate the character. The voice was supposed to come later, from someone more famous. At the 11th hour, it was his.

According to recent reports, born in Albany and raised in Texas, the Puerto Rican and Italian artist trained classically at Purchase College and found puppetry when the acting jobs didn’t come. His first agent told him he wouldn’t work until he was 40. He turned 40 a couple of months before cameras rolled. Onstage, he won an Obie for “The Woodsman,” designed the puppets for Lincoln Center’s “The Skin of Our Teeth” and created Milky White, the scene-stealing cow of the 2022 Broadway revival of “Into the Woods.” “Project Hail Mary” is his first film.

Recent findings suggest that what strikes me is how plainly he describes the work as acting. He breaks down a script the way he once broke down Prospero and Oberon. The only difference, he indicates, is that he funnels those choices “through an external shell.” That’s why the conversation around him matters.

According to recent reports, we’ve had versions of this debate before, with Frank Oz’s Yoda, Andy Serkis’ Gollum and Zoe Saldaña in “Avatar.” Ortiz is eligible for both the Oscars and the Actor Awards, where SAG-AFTRA covers puppeteers. In theater, he points out, puppeteers are most often classified as crew.

He isn’t campaigning for a trophy so much as for recognition of a craft. “The goal is to create a character that you get lost in,” he notes. “But I think there’s value in talking about the folks that made that.”.

Excerpts from the episode, edited and condensed for clarity, are below.

The way we approached making that thing, even though it was my first film ever, felt, from what I understand, quite avant-garde. In a funny way, it felt like I was doing some downtown play every day. But I left every day going, “I don’t really know what we just made.” There was such an emphasis on crafting and improvising on the take that there were so many different versions of every single second of that film. So two years of waiting was pretty brutal.

I was so pleased and surprised when I got to see the final thing, especially when, at the 11th hour, I was told I was going to be the voice. And then the studio and the team stated, “Why don’t we talk about this?” That’s a really unusual thing for suit performers and mocap and puppeteers.

My goal was always to be an actor. I went through this classical training program at Purchase, and it was all Shakespeare and Chekhov, all the things I’m still really passionate about. Then it’s that funny thing: What do you do with that information? How do you sell cereal? How do you do a bite and smile?

The first agent I signed with, in my early 20s, the ink was literally still wet on the contract, said, “You know, you’re not going to work until you’re 40.” And I turned 40 a couple of months before we started shooting “Hail Mary.” Isn’t that nuts? So maybe he was right. Who cares?

Recent findings suggest that I was always drawn to painting and drawing and sculpting. My father was always engineering and tinkering and building things in the house. My mother is an academic, really literary and taught me about story structure. Long story short, all of those elements go directly into puppetry. I loved acting, performing, directing, engineering and fine art and it felt like I gamed the system by finding something where I didn’t have to pick one. When the acting gigs weren’t coming in, one thing accidentally led to another. I stated, “Yeah, I can do that for this wacky downtown show for $200″ and it kick-started this thing.

Sources indicate that it’s become a way for me to play characters I would never, ever be cast as. That’s the thing I found about puppetry: It ends up being the most freeing form of acting because I don’t have to start from how you perceive me.

On any other role I’ve played, sans puppet, I would have ripped the script apart trying to figure out who this soul is. How do they think? How do they love? What are they terrified of? Then the exercise becomes how you funnel that through your human shell, physically and emotionally. The only difference with puppetry is that I’m funneling it through an external shell. I’m doing all of the homework.

According to recent reports, my approach, maybe because I started as an actor, whether it was creating Milky White on Broadway or “The Skin of Our Teeth” for Lincoln Center or the operas I’m doing, was always: What do we want the audience to feel? The precision will come later. This is a tool to play a character that should not be played by a person. So let’s take advantage of it. Let’s not let it be pedestrian.

I was originally going to play the puppet entirely by myself on set. Then we saw the scale of it and how many legs he had. We knew that from the book, but seeing the puppet, I raised my hand and remarked, “Guys, I do a lot of ensemble puppetry and ensemble direction in my theatrical career. I would love to bring in other local puppet artists and build a team.” Not people who are just there to hold a leg. I needed to get them inside my head so we could play this character together.

According to recent reports, for about eight weeks before we shot, we focused on how to use movement to express subtext. This is a character coming from a pretty traumatic 80 years alone in space. This character has never been alone before in their life. They’re a eusocial species, so they truly don’t know what it is to be solo. How does that existential pain manifest physically? That’s the delicious stuff. And I’m making it sound like we did a Bergman film. There was a lot of humor and silliness, but all of that has to come from something that feels grounded.

This might sound a little crazy, but there is no such thing, especially on film, as an actor’s performance being entirely their own. NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.
  • Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m.
  • NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft debuted almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft debuted almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

Sources indicate that it flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

Industry observers note that the spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

Sources indicate that but if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy.
  • Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words.
  • The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A latest study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

Sources indicate that "The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy highlights up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction.".

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy.

It has been revealed that the researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about crucial moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

Recent findings suggest that after writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language.

In a recent development, participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, demonstrated a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

Sources indicate that these differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane remarked. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life.".

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes.

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

In a recent development, this variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

Sources indicate that "People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray noted. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

It has been revealed that "Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships.".

It has been revealed that like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment.

Industry observers note that recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane mentioned. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict crucial outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict.".

According to recent reports, researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

Recent findings suggest that "If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”.

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put new restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the glitch of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

Sources indicate that that’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

In a recent development, but Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, remarked that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about looks to speak out?

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

According to recent reports, the CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

According to recent reports, so is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the issues that need addressing.

The nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

They’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

It sounds like CEOs are frustrated?

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

You would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from substantial business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and announced it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.

Sources indicate that those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston noted, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".

Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy.".

"They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this firm," he stated. "At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth.".

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.

"The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston said. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded.".

Recent findings suggest that the company will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

Here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:.

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

The firm's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.

In a recent development, disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.

The division is already a top performer for the tech giant, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.

While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston mentioned.

In a recent development, growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro stated he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with new additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

"Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he stated. "And new capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits.".

The firm expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

Sources indicate that over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney mentioned.

The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the company saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5.".

Disney said Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

According to recent reports, the tech giant's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.

Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

In a recent development, the company expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the Newly introduced Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.

Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.

D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the manufacturer's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.

In a recent development, "Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro said on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses.".

Disney announced a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.

D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.

"There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he noted. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that looks and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World.".

The entertainment tech giant has also expanded its short-form content, adding a vertical video channel within the Disney+ mobile app. The company had previously unveiled a partnership with TikTok to bring creator content to the streaming app.

The president had also sparked backlash for his efforts to overhaul the Kennedy Center, including adding his name to the exterior, which are still playing out in court.

Those involved with the film and series downplayed any significance of the change in venue, noting the president and first lady’s ties to New York. The screening came just two weeks after the 2026 midterm elections saw Democrats score historic, surprise victories in a referendum on the president that will result in a change in party control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Still, Trump’s longtime adviser Marc Beckman previously teased that the docuseries, now streaming on Amazon’s Prime Video, would be a “total different experience, completely fresh.”.

Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of the Melania: The Series premiere, Beckman explained how the filmmaking team determined what would go in the documentary and what would be for the series.

Recent findings suggest that “We decided that we would bifurcate and isolate certain stories that we thought were suitable for the series that weren’t necessarily appropriate for the film,” Beckman said. “The reason they’re suitable for the series is because it gives us more time to unpack more of her storyline, more about her family, more about her career, more about philanthropy and also what happens right after the inauguration when she takes on the role of being first lady of the United States again.”.

Melania: The Series producer Fernando Sulichin, who took on the same role on the documentary, added that the film “was about going into the inauguration, and this one is first lady in action and what she’s about, more intimate — not the preparation of becoming the first lady but being the first lady.”.

Beckman likened the approach to what Trump’s team did with her 2024 self-titled memoir Melania.

“With the trade edition of the book, we tell the story and we have certain photos in it, and then the collector’s edition, it’s a completely different experience so the fans could get both and enjoy them,” he remarked. “That’s the same thing here.”.

Though it was initially expected that the docuseries would arrive on Amazon’s Prime Video when the documentary began streaming in March, Beckman mentioned that was “just the media speculating,” and insisted the timing of the series’ release was in keeping with the licensing deal with Amazon he negotiated for the film and series.

“The timing for the contract is exactly what we’ve done,” he told THR on the black carpet Thursday night. “I negotiated the contract, so trust me, there’s no delay.”.

While the documentary film, which was released in theaters in late January, followed Trump in the two weeks leading up to the start of her husband’s second term as president, the docuseries, in which Trump answers softball questions about her daily routine, interests and beliefs, first focuses on her role as a wife and mother, including her relationship with the president, followed by an episode centered around her and the president’s trips to North Carolina in the wake of Hurricane Helene and Los Angeles after the 2025 wildfires.

It has been revealed that the film, coming in the wake of Trump’s best-selling memoir, was seen as part of a launch of a lifestyle brand. The doc and series’ $40 million Amazon purchase sparked backlash that the tech giant was trying to curry favor with the White House, criticism likely to continue with the project’s latest extension.

And while the Lincoln Center screening boasted Trump’s signature black-and-white color palette, complete with a black carpet and white tables and flowers, as well as tickets and popcorn boxes featuring the first lady’s face, Beckman steered questions about a possible lifestyle tech giant back to Trump’s humanitarian efforts, specifically her work brokering a ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine and her Fostering the Future initiative to provide resources and educational opportunities for foster kids.

Recent findings suggest that “I think right now what she’s really proud of is how she’s helping children and people throughout the world,” Beckman noted. “What she’s doing in America is so much more important than a lifestyle brand.”.

And before the docuseries premiered, Trump spoke, from a black-and-white podium bearing her name, about the Ukraine ceasefire, connecting it to her own personal ethos and the series’ focus, and episode titles, of “Family & Trust” and “Pride & Honor.”.

“We live in a world that never stops moving, but life’s greatest moments belong to those who can stand still,” she began. “In calmness, we can see beauty. In peace, we can see humanity. My work is demanding, and sometimes the challenges I face seem impossible. Still, even in the most difficult circumstances, I find the drive to achieve the impossible. I rely on my own strength and character, with conviction, courage and reckless determination. I found a way forward where others would not.”.

In a recent development, “For a brief moment, the world stood still for Oleshky. Eight hundred lives were saved. After so many years of fighting, the ceasefire brought a little bit of sunshine into lives which had been in the shadows of fear and war. The moment was very powerful for me because fighting and conflict have no value to the families on either side. Peace is rational,” she continued. “In the Oleshky ceasefire, we see the power of family, the restoration of trust and the courage of young children who do not back down in the face of war. Family, trust, pride, honor are the values we all hold in our hearts; they are also the foundation of the personal story I’m going to share with you tonight as part of Melania: The Series.”.

As Trump teased that the series offered the opportunity to “experience [her] world through a latest lens,” Trump’s current and former colleagues remarked they hoped the show, like the documentary, let Trump tell her own story.

President Trump’s first-term adviser Kellyanne Conway said conceptually that the documentary and series were “so amazing.”.

Industry observers note that “She’s obviously a very private person who has a very public life and in my view a very positive impact and that story does not get told,” Conway told THR. “And that’s OK, so let her tell her own story.”.

Recent findings suggest that fashion designer Hervé Pierre, who created the first lady’s inaugural gowns for the president’s first and second ceremonies, added, “She’s not mysterious, but she’s not all over the media all the time and I think when she does something like she just did with [Russia and Ukraine], it’s not, like, fluff. It’s a very specific mission. So I think it’s crucial. I hope we will discover something that we don’t know about her. And I think sometimes it’s better for her to [express something in her own words] than to have an interpretation of what she’s doing. At least you have a direct line.”.

And what sort of things might viewers discover about Trump that they don’t already know?

Pierre, who’s long worked with the first lady, offered a couple of insights.

“She cries when she laughs,” he remarked of her tendency to tear up at humorous moments. “She’s very happy. I’ve worked with difficult women for 30 years in haute couture. She never, ever raised her voice or [had attitude]. She’s always in a good mood — it’s fascinating.”.

#24558. Industry News: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
